Consult Summary:
- 50-year-old woman with 5–6 days of a continuous dry cough, rhinorrhea, chills with myalgias, transient diarrhea, and fatigue; clinician assessment: likely viral upper respiratory infection, advised symptomatic care and follow-up if not improving.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Continuous, persistent dry cough for ~5–6 days, worse at night and disturbing sleep; causing sore throat/irritation from coughing.
  - Runny nose (rhinorrhea) beginning at same time.
  - Chills/shivering and generalized muscle aches since onset; patient felt feverish but did not measure temperature.
  - Transient diarrhea at onset (started with cough), resolved after the first day.
  - Lethargy/tiredness; no significant baseline exertional shortness of breath (only breathless when actively coughing).
- Timeline/progression:
  - Symptoms began approximately 5–6 days ago.
  - Diarrhea lasted only at the beginning and has resolved.
  - Cough and rhinorrhea have persisted and remain bothersome; patient reports not yet improving.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Cough continuous throughout day and night; no specific exacerbating factors identified.
  - Rest and fluids recommended by clinician as supportive care.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems:
  - No sputum production (dry cough).
  - Throat soreness attributable to coughing; no odynophagia with swallowing.
  - No ear pain, blockage, or discharge.
  - No chest pain.
  - No baseline dyspnea on exertion; no new chronic breathlessness.
  - No nausea or vomiting.
  - Urinary symptoms absent; adequate urine output reported after initial increased fluid intake during diarrhea.
  - No skin rash reported.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No productive cough, hemoptysis, or chest pain.
  - No vomiting, persistent abdominal pain, or ongoing diarrhea.
  - Partner at home is asymptomatic.

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus — patient reports regular follow-up with a doctor; medication: Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Hypertension — patient reports it is controlled; medication: Lisinopril (patient report) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Conflict noted: clinician said "Zinopril" in the encounter; patient explicitly stated "Lisinopril." (Conflict documented below.)
- Allergies: none reported.

Social History:
- Living situation: lives with partner; partner currently well.
- Occupation: software developer (IT), generally sedentary job.
- Work status: missed one day of work initially, returned to work thereafter; advised to consider 1–2 days off if able.
- Tobacco: former smoker; quit approximately 6 months ago.
- Alcohol: drinks wine about 2–3 evenings per week, typically 2–3 glasses per occasion; clinician advised reduction (specific plan offered: reduce to two glasses/week for a trial period then reassess).
- Substance use: none reported.

Family History:
- Father with type 2 diabetes mellitus; no other family history reported.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: not documented.
- Examination findings: not documented.

Investigations:
- No laboratory tests, imaging, or diagnostic studies were performed or documented in the encounter.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Acute viral upper respiratory infection (probable) presenting with dry cough, rhinorrhea, chills, myalgias, transient diarrhea, and fatigue.
  - Assessment: Clinician believes this is likely viral and self-limited; typical duration ~7–10 days.
  - Plan:
    - Symptomatic management: rest, maintain hydration.
    - Analgesic/antipyretic recommended: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
    - Advice to take 1–2 days off work if possible to rest and reduce potential transmission.
    - Return precautions: re-evaluate if not improving in 2–3 days; return sooner if breathing worsens or cough/fever persist/worsen.
    - If still febrile and cough not improving on re-evaluation, clinician may consider antibiotics for suspected bacterial chest infection at that time.
- Issue 2: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (chronic comorbidity).
  - Assessment: Patient reports ongoing regular primary care follow-up; no acute changes reported.
  - Plan:
    - Continue current diabetes care and follow-up as per usual (no medication changes documented).
- Issue 3: Hypertension (chronic comorbidity).
  - Assessment: Patient reports hypertension is controlled on current therapy; no acute changes reported.
  - Plan:
    - Continue current antihypertensive therapy (Lisinopril per patient) and routine follow-up (no changes documented).
- General plan items:
  - Advise alcohol reduction given diabetes and hypertension; clinician suggested an initial reduction strategy (patient education only).
  - Advise prompt re-assessment if respiratory symptoms worsen, breathing becomes more labored, or fever persists.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs (temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation) not documented.
  - Physical examination findings (lung auscultation, throat exam) not documented.
  - Medication doses, routes, and frequencies for chronic meds (Metformin, Lisinopril) and symptomatic med (Paracetamol) not documented.
  - No diagnostic testing documented (e.g., rapid viral testing, COVID/influenza test, chest radiograph) which may be clinically expected for persistent cough or fever depending on local protocols.
  - No recent diabetes control metrics (e.g., HbA1c) documented.
- Internal conflicts from the transcript:
  - Medication name conflict: patient states she takes Lisinopril for blood pressure; clinician at one point says “Zinopril.” Conflict noted.
- Transcript quality:
  - Conversation largely clear and intelligible; some minor interruptions/overlaps but overall adequate for clinical documentation.
